title: 1 Introduction
content: Introduction. to Organizational Behaviour MN 4063: Organizational Behaviour & Management Nadeesha Perera Faculty of Engineering University of Moratuwa contents. Meaning of work Functions of work Alienation What is OB? OB in simple terms Core topics of OB Multidisciplinary nature of OB Beginning of OB Absolutes in OB The organizational iceberg Management as an integrating activity Implications for managers Meaning of Work What does “work” mean to you? Meaning of Work Work could be more meaningfully defined as an activity that produces something of value for other people. Functions of Work • Work serves a rather obvious economic function. • Work serves several social functions. • Work provides a source of social status in the community. • Work can be an important source of identity, self-esteem, and, for some, a means for self- actualisation. Work and Self- Esteem • Work contributes to self-esteem in at least two ways. It provides individuals with an opportunity to demonstrate competence mastery over themselves and their environment. Individuals discover that they can actually do something. Work reassures individuals that they are carrying out activities that produce something of value to others-that they have something significant to offer. Alienation If your work doesn't provide you with any of these functions, you will often experience sensations of powerlessness, meaninglessness, and normlessness-a condition called alienation. What is OB? Organizational behaviour (OB) is a field of study that investigates the impact individuals, groups, and structure have on behaviour within organizations, to apply such knowledge toward improving an organization's effectiveness. OB in Simple Terms • Simply, OB is the study of what people do organization and how their behaviour affects the organization's performance. • OB's goal is to understand and predict human behaviour in organizations. OB in Simple Terms • The complexities of human behaviour are not easy predict, but neither are they random-certain fundamental consistencies underlie the behaviour of all individuals. • OB studies three determinants of behaviour in organizations: individuals, groups, and structure. Core Topics of OB • Motivation • Leader behaviour and power • Interpersonal communication • Group structure and processes • Attitude development and perception • Change processes • Conflict and negotiation • Work design Multidisciplinary Nature of OB • OB is an applied behavioural science built on contributions from several behavioural disciplines, mainly psychology and social psychology, sociology, anthropology, and, increasingly, political science and neuroscience. • Several social science disciplines contribute to OB, but none are more important than psychology. Multidisciplinary Nature of OB • Sociology explores how society shapes people. It helps us understand that no action takes place in a social vacuum and helps us appreciate how individual experiences are part of broader society. • Psychology seeks to measure, explain, and sometimes change human behaviour. It is often considered the science of the mind. Multidisciplinary Nature of OB • Social psychology bridges sociology and psychology, and tries to understand the impact the group has on the outlook of the individual. • Anthropology examines rites and rituals that shape how groups and cultures work. • Political science examines the role of power within organizations. Beginnings of OB • Organizational behaviour distinct discipline started when scientific approaches management began indicate that behavioural considerations were important predictors of productivity. The famous Hawthorne studies were conducted between and Hawthorne Electrical Company. Hawthorne Studies • Elton Mayo's and Fritz Roethlisberger's Hawthorne Studies is considered to be a milestone in Management Sciences. Hawthorne Studies A series of experiments on worker productivity begun in 1924 at the Hawthorne plant of Western Electric company Illinois; attributed employees' increased output managers' better treatment of them during the study. Hawthorne Studies Original Findings: Money was not the cause of the increased output. Employees performed better when managers treated them in a positive manner ( Human relations). Hawthorne Studies Recent analysis: Money mattered a great deal at Hawthorne. In addition, Worker productivity increased partly as a result of the increased feeling of importance and 'group pride' employees felt by being selected for this important project. Hawthorne Studies Hawthorne effect: Subjects behaved differently because of the active participation of the researchers in the Hawthorne experiments. Absolutes in OB • Laws in the physical sciences-chemistry, astronomy, physics-are consistent and apply in various situations. • However, Humans are complex; because we are not all alike, our ability to make simple, accurate, and sweeping generalizations is limited. Absolutes in OB • It does mean that OB concepts must reflect situational, or contingency, conditions. • We can say x leads to y, but only under conditions specified in z-the contingency variables. • The science of OB was developed by applying general concepts to a particular situation, person, or group. The Organizational Iceberg One way to recognise why people behave as they do at work is to view an organisation as an iceberg. What sinks ships isn't always what sailors can see, but what they can't see. Hellriegel et al. The Organizational Iceberg The Organizational Iceberg • The overt, formal aspects focus only on the tip of the iceberg (organisation). • It is just as important to focus on what you can't see - the covert, behavioural aspects. These are the activities of people, which affect both the productivity and quality of the working life of an organisation. The Organizational Iceberg • The biggest challenge we face when trying to analyse or manage organisations is that they do not actually exist. The Organizational Iceberg The organisation in which you work or study is not something you can see, hear, touch, smell, kick, kiss or throw up in the air. And this is not just because you might be a relatively junior member of that organisation. The top managers of the organisation are no more capable than you are of relating to the organisation as if it existed in a straightforward way. This, in fact, is one of the most fascinating aspects of organisational and managerial work - and its essential ambiguity. Management as an Integrating Activity • Whatever the individual's orientation to work, the nature of the work organisation or cultural influences, it is through the process of management that the efforts of members of the organisation are co- ordinated, directed and guided towards the achievement of its goals. Management as an Integrating Activity • Unlike physical resources, the people resource is not owned by the organisation. • People bring their own perceptions, feelings and attitudes towards the organisation, systems and styles of management, their duties and responsibilities, and the conditions under which they are working. Management as an Integrating Activity • At the heart of successful management is the problem of integrating the individual and the organisation, and this requires an understanding of both human personality and work organisations. Implications for Managers Use scientifically validated information about human behaviour to help improve your interpersonal skills in the workplace. This will increase your leadership potential. Use metrics and situational variables rather than “hunches” to explain cause-and-effect relationships. Improve your technical skills and conceptual skills through training and staying current with OB trends like big data. Implications for Managers • OB can improve your employees' work quality and productivity by showing you how to empower your employees, design and implement change programs, improve customer service, and help your employees balance work-life conflicts. • Use caution when applying research international contexts; some of the underlying cultural norms and expectations may vary, altering results. Implications for Managers • Recognize that human behaviour in the workplace is influenced by factors at three different levels: individual, group, and organizational. Paying attention to relevant factors at all three levels rather than focusing on just one can improve management effectiveness. summary.

title: 2 Attitudes
content: Understanding Yourself & Others: Attitudes. & Job Satisfaction MN 4063: Organizational Behaviour & Management Nadeesha Perera Faculty of Engineering University of Moratuwa contents. • Recognition of individuality • Attitudes • Beliefs and values • Main components of attitude • Behavioural justification • Major job attitudes • Job satisfaction • Other job attitudes Recognition of Individuality • The individual is a central feature of organisational behaviour. • Organisations are made their individual members, whether acting isolation or as part of a group, in response to expectations of the organisation, or as a result of the influences of the external environment. Recognition of Individuality • Individual differences can foster creativity, enjoyment and satisfaction at work but can also be the potential for conflict and frustration. • Managers are required to be competent at selecting and developing individuals who will be valuable to the organisation. Recognition of Individuality • Managers need to know themselves and understand their uniqueness and the impact of their own personality on others. • Managing relationships at work has always been a key skill, but the speed of change in organisations and the external environment places increasing pressure on individuals at work. Recognition of Individuality • When change appears externally imposed, the management of people takes on different dimension terms the sensitivity required. • Such changes may lead to new mindsets, attitudes and perceptions that enable people to cope with and adjust to the different world. Recognition of Individuality • Managers will be expected to understand the strains employees feel during times of change, but at the same time deal with their own levels of stress. Recognition of Individuality Individuals differ in terms of, Ethnic origin Physique Gender Early family experiences Social and cultural factors National culture Motivation Attitudes Personality traits and types Intelligence and abilities Perception Attitudes • Simply, how a person perceives the world around him/her. • Attitude how person views and evaluates something someone, predisposition or a tendency to respond positively or negatively toward a certain idea, object, person, or situation. Attitudes When you say “I like my job,” you are expressing your attitude about work. How Attitudes are Formed? • There is considerable disagreement about this question. • Three popular views in this regard are, 1. Dispositional approach 2. Situational approach 3. Social-information-processing approach 1. Dispositional approach Psychologist Barry Staw and others argue that attitudes represent relatively stable predispositions to respond to people or situations around them. That is, attitudes are viewed almost as personality traits. Thus, some people would have tendency-a predisposition-to be happy on the job, almost regardless of the nature of the work itself. 1. Dispositional approach • Others may have an internal tendency to be unhappy, again almost regardless of the actual nature of the work. • Evidence in support of this approach can be found in a series of studies that found that attitudes change very little among people before and after they make a job change. 2. Situational approach • This approach argues that attitudes emerge as a result of the uniqueness of a given situation. • They are situationally determined and can vary in response to changing work conditions. • Thus, as a result of experiences at work (a boring or unrewarding job, a bad supervisor, etc.), people react by developing appropriate attitudes. 3. Social-information-processing approach • This view, developed Pfeffer and Salancik, asserts that attitudes result from “socially constructed realities” as perceived by the individual. • That is, the social context in which the individual is placed shapes his perceptions of the situation and hence his attitudes. 3. Social-information-processing approach Which Approach is Correct? • In point of fact, research indicates that both the dispositional and the social information-processing views have merit, and probably wise recognize that socially constructed realities and dispositions interact to form the basis for individual's attitudes at work. Beliefs & Values • Beliefs are concerned with what is known about the world; they centre on what 'is', on reality as it is understood. Values are concerned with what 'should' be and what is desirable. Main Components of Attitude Attitudes have three components: Cognition Affect Behaviour Main Components of Attitude Main Components of Attitude- Cognition • A description of or belief in the way things are. E.g.: The statement “My pay is low” is the cognitive component of an attitude. Main Components of Attitude- Affect • Affect is the emotional or feeling segment attitude. E.g.: “I am angry over how little I'm paid.” Main Components of Attitude- Behaviour This component of an attitude describes an intention to behave in a certain way toward someone or something. E.g.: “I'm going to look for another job that pays better”. Main Components of Attitude • These components are closely related, and cognition and affect in particular are inseparable in many ways. • Read the next scenario to understand the interrelationship among components of attitude. Main Components of Attitude An employee didn't get a promotion he thought he deserved; a coworker got it instead. The employee's attitude toward his supervisor illustrated follows: The employee thought deserved the promotion (cognition), he strongly dislikes his supervisor (affect), and he has complained and taken action (behaviour). Main Components of Attitude • Although we often think cognition causes affect, which then causes behaviour, in reality, these components are difficult to separate. • To put it another way, we don't always fully understand our own attitudes and actions, and the explanations we come up with for our own behaviour might sometimes be inaccurate as a result. Behavioural Justification • People often feel a need for behavioural justification ensure that their behaviours are consistent with their attitudes toward the event- Cognitive consistency Behavioural Justification Effects cognitive dissonance- any incompatibility individual might perceive between two more attitudes between behaviour and attitudes. Behavioural Justification • When people find themselves acting in a fashion that is inconsistent with their attitudes-when they experience cognitive dissonance-they experience tension and attempt reduce this tension and return to a state of cognitive consistency. Major Job Attitudes • Individuals have many kinds of attitudes about their jobs. • Of the main job attitudes, job satisfaction, job involvement and organizational commitment are the most widely studied. • Other important attitudes include perceived organizational support, employee engagement and citizenship behaviour. Job Satisfaction • A positive feeling about a job, resulting from an evaluation of its characteristics. person with high level job satisfaction holds positive feelings about his job, while a person with a low level holds negative feelings. Job Satisfaction • Jobs require interacting with coworkers and bosses, following organizational rules and policies, meeting performance standards, living with less-than-ideal working conditions, and the like. employee's assessment his satisfaction with the job is thus a complex summation of many distinct elements. Characteristics of Job Satisfaction Satisfaction is an emotional response to a job situation. Job satisfaction is perhaps best understood in terms of discrepancy. Job expectation Vs. Job outcome To the extent that the outcomes received by an employee meet or exceed expectations, we would expect the employee to be satisfied with the job and wish to remain. Dimensions of Job Satisfaction Research has suggested that five job dimensions represent the most salient characteristics of a job about which people have affective responses. 1. Work itself The extent to which tasks performed by employees are interesting and provide opportunities for learning and for accepting responsibility. Dimensions of Job Satisfaction 2. Pay The amount of pay received, the perceived equity of the pay, and the method of payment. 3. Promotional opportunities The availability realistic opportunities for advancement. Dimensions of Job Satisfaction 4. Supervision The technical and managerial abilities of supervisors; the extent to which supervisors demonstrate consideration for and interest in employees. 5. Coworkers The extent to which coworkers are friendly, technically competent, and supportive. Dimensions of Job Satisfaction Measurement of Job Satisfaction • Satisfaction is considered by many managers important indicator organizational effectiveness, and therefore it is regularly monitored to assess employee feelings toward the organization. • By far the most common means of assessing satisfaction is the rating scale. Measurement of Job Satisfaction • Although rating scales have many virtues compared to other techniques, at least 2 drawbacks must be recognized. As with any self-report inventory, it is assumed that respondents are both willing and able to describe their feelings accurately. The underlying assumption that questionnaire items mean the same thing to all people. Impact of Satisfied/Dissatisfied Employees on the Workplace The exit-voice- loyalty-neglect framework helps understand the consequences dissatisfaction. Other Job Attitudes- Job Involvement • Job involvement refers to the extent to which a person is interested in and committed to assigned tasks. Employees with a high level of job involvement strongly identify with and really care about the kind of work they do. Other Job Attitudes- Job Involvement • Psychological empowerment refers employees' beliefs in the degree to which they influence their work environments, their competencies, the meaningfulness of their jobs, and their perceived autonomy. Other Job Attitudes- Organizational Commitment • Relative strength of an individual's identification with and involvement in an organization. • Commitment can be characterized by 3 factors: (1) a strong belief in and acceptance of the organization's goals and values, (2) a willingness to exert considerable effort on behalf of the organization, and (3) a strong desire to maintain membership in the organization. Other Job Attitudes- Organizational Commitment • Commitment represents something beyond mere passive loyalty the company. • Most research has focused on emotional attachment to an organization and belief in its values as the “gold standard” for employee commitment. Other Job Attitudes- Perceived Organizational Support • This is the degree to which employees believe the organization values their contributions and cares about their well-being. • Research shows that people perceive their organizations as supportive when rewards are deemed fair, when employees have a voice in decisions, and when they see their supervisors as supportive. Other Job Attitudes- Perceived Organizational Support • Employees with strong POS perceptions have been found more likely to have higher levels of citizenship behaviours, lower levels of tardiness, and better customer service. Other Job Attitudes- Employee Engagement • An individual's involvement with, satisfaction with, and enthusiasm for, the work he/she does. • Highly engaged employees have a passion for their work and feel a deep connection to their companies; disengaged employees have essentially checked out-putting time but not energy or attention into their work. Other Job Attitudes- Employee Engagement • Engagement becomes a real concern for most organizations because surveys indicate that few employees-between 17 % and 29%-are highly engaged in their work. Other Job Attitudes- Organizational Citizenship Behaviour • Organizational citizenship behaviours (OCBs) are individual, discretionary actions by employees that are outside their formal job description. • Employees who feel organizational citizenship will “go the extra mile” out of personal motivation - identifying these motivations can lead to increased performance and job satisfaction. Other Job Attitudes- Organizational Citizenship Behaviour • Positive OCBs reduce the need for supervision, improve workplace morale and result in cost-saving suggestions - all of which free up managerial time. Managers who are aware of the pros and cons of OCBs can help employees contribute optimally to the organization and avoid burnout. Are these Job Attitudes really All that Distinct? There some distinctiveness among attitudes, but they overlap greatly for various reasons, including the employee's personality.

title: 3 Personality
content: Understanding Yourself & Others: Personality. MN 4063: Organizational Behaviour & Management Nadeesha Perera Faculty of Engineering University of Moratuwa contents. • Personality • Personality determinants • Dominant personality frameworks • Other Personality Frameworks • Personality and situations • Values • Linking values to individual personality at the workplace • International values Personality • Personality may be viewed as consisting of stable characteristics and traits that explain why a person behaves in a particular way. for instance, independence, conscientiousness, agreeableness and self- control are examples personality characteristics. Personality Determinants Hereditary: • These are the factors that are determined at conception/origin. Personality Determinants • Physical stature, facial features, gender, temperament, muscle composition and reflexes, energy level, and biological rhythms are generally considered to be either completely substantially influenced parentage-by your biological parents' genetic, physiological, and psychological makeup. Personality Determinants • The hereditary approach argues that the ultimate explanation of an individual's personality is the molecular structure of the genes, located in the chromosomes. • Personality changes in the course of a lifetime. Personality Determinants • Research has shown that personality is more changeable in adolescence and more stable among adults. • When someone exhibits certain personality characteristic/s large number of situations, we call them the “personality traits” of that person. Personality Determinants • The more consistent the characteristic over time, and the more frequently it occurs in diverse situations, the more important that trait is in describing the individual. Dominant Personality Frameworks • There are mainly 2 dominant frameworks for assessing an individual's personality traits. 1. The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator 2. The Big Five Model The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (mbti) • mbti. the most widely used personality-assessment instrument the world. It is a 100-question personality test that asks people how they usually feel or act in situations. The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) Extraverted Versus Introverted Extraverted individuals are outgoing, sociable, and assertive. Introverts are quiet and shy. Sensing (S) Versus Intuitive (N). Sensing types are practical, prefer routine and order, and focus on details. Intuitives rely on unconscious processes and look at the “big picture.” The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) Thinking (T) Versus Feeling (F). Thinking types use reason and logic to handle problems. Feeling types rely on their personal values and emotions. Judging (J) Versus Perceiving (P). Judging types want to control and prefer order and structure. Perceiving types are flexible and spontaneous. The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) • These classifications describe personality types by identifying one trait from each of the four pairs. Why the Myers-Briggs test is totally meaningless? The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) Some psychologists find inconsistencies in the MBTI's theoretical framework. The theory assumes that personality static and doesn't consider the possibility that people can, and often do, develop and change over time. The Big Five Model • The Big Five personality traits are related to many OB criteria; each of the five traits has proven its usefulness in understanding individual behaviour in organizations. • These are the big five factors, The Big Five Model- Extraversion The extraversion dimension captures our comfort level with relationships. Extraverts tend gregarious, assertive, and sociable. Introverts tend to be reserved, timid, and quiet. This dimension also refers to preferred stimulation levels. The Big Five Model-Extraversion • Introverts tend to become overwhelmed when there are a lot of stimuli in the environment (such as a large, busy party), and they may seek a quiet place to recover from the excess sensory input, while extroverts are energized and excited by busy environments. The Big Five Model- Agreeableness • The agreeableness dimension refers to an individual's propensity to defer to others. • Highly agreeable people are cooperative, warm, and trusting. • People who score low on agreeableness are cold, disagreeable, and antagonistic. The Big Five Model- Conscientiousness • The conscientiousness dimension measure of reliability. • A highly conscientious person is responsible, organized, dependable, and persistent. • Those who score low on this dimension are easily distracted, disorganized, and unreliable. The Big Five Model- Emotional stability • The emotional stability dimension-often labelled by its converse, neuroticism-taps a person's ability to withstand stress. • People with positive emotional stability tend to be calm, self-confident, and secure. Those with high negative scores tend to be nervous, anxious, depressed, and insecure. The Big Five Model- Openness to experience • The openness experience dimension addresses range interests and fascination with novelty. • Open people are creative, curious, and artistically sensitive. • Those at the other end of the category are conventional and find comfort in the familiar. The Big Five Model Other Personality Frameworks • Research indicates the Big Five traits have the most verifiable linkages important organizational outcomes, but they are neither the only traits a person exhibits nor the only ones with organizational behaviour implications. • Researchers have found that three other socially undesirable traits, which we all have in varying degrees, are relevant organizational behaviour:Dark Triad Other Personality Frameworks-Machiavellianism • The personality characteristic Machiavellianism (often abbreviated Mach) is named after Niccolo Machiavelli, who wrote in the 16th century on how to gain and use power. • An individual high in Machiavellianism is pragmatic, maintains emotional distance, and believes ends can justify means. Other Personality Frameworks-Machiavellianism • “If it works, use it” is consistent with a high-Mach perspective. • A considerable amount of research has found that high Machs manipulate more, win more, and encourage others more than low Machs. Other Personality Frameworks-Machiavellianism • They are more likely to act aggressively and engage in other counterproductive work behaviours. • High-Mach employees, manipulating others to their advantage, may win in the short term, but they lose those gains in the long term because they are not well-liked. Other Personality Frameworks-Narcissism • The trait is named for the Greek myth of Narcissus, a youth so vain and proud he fell in love with his own image. • In psychology, narcissism describes a person who has grandiose sense self- importance, requires excessive admiration, has a sense of entitlement, and is arrogant. Other Personality Frameworks-Narcissism • Evidence suggests narcissists are more charismatic than others. • Both leaders and managers tend to score higher on narcissism, suggesting that certain self- centeredness is needed to succeed. • Some evidence suggests that narcissists are more adaptable and make better business decisions than others when the decision is complex. Other Personality Frameworks-Narcissism • Some people believe that camera phones and social media encourage narcissism. • Among people who believe that the “selfies” trend is considered a sign of widespread, excessive, narcissism. Other Personality Frameworks- Psychopathy • In the OB context, psychopathy is defined as a lack of concern for others and a lack of guilt or remorse when their actions cause harm. Measures of psychopathy attempt to assess the person's motivation to comply with social norms; willingness to use deceit to obtain desired ends and the effectiveness of those efforts; impulsivity; and disregard, that is, lack of empathic concern, for others. Other Personality Frameworks- Psychopathy • From an organisational perspective, a psychopath in the workplace presents themselves as being hireable and worthy promotion, intelligent, smooth charming, manipulative, happy to take others' work as their own, opportunistic, calculating and operating without remorse. Other Personality Frameworks- Psychopathy • Research has found that psychopaths can be found across all levels of the organisation including high percentage being leadership positions. A corporate psychopath uses instrumental bullying to further his goals of promotion and power as the result of causing confusion and 'divide and rule'. Other Personality Frameworks- Psychopathy • The research suggests that psychopathy is related to the use of hard influence tactics (threats, manipulation) and bullying work behaviour (physical or verbal threatening). Other Personality Frameworks- Psychopathy • There are 2 types of bullying, i.e. 1. Predatory bullying - the bully just enjoys bullying and tormenting vulnerable people for the sake of it. 2. Instrumental bullying - the bullying is for a purpose, helping the bully achieve his or her goals. Other Personality Frameworks- Psychopathy • The cunning displayed by people who score high on psychopathy may help them gain power in an organization, but keep them from using that power toward healthy ends for themselves or their organizations. Other Personality Frameworks Personality & Situations • The effect particular traits organizational behaviour depends on the situation. • Two theoretical frameworks include, 1. Situation strength 2. Trait activation theory (TAT) Situation Strength This theory proposes that the way personality translates into behaviour depends on the strength of the situation. Situation strength means the degree to which norms, cues, or standards dictate appropriate behaviour. Situation Strength • Strong situations pressure us to exhibit the right behaviour, clearly show us what that behaviour is, and discourage the wrong behaviour. Research suggests that personality traits better predict behaviour weak situations than in strong ones. Situation Strength Aspects personality including attention- seeking, conservatism, and risk tolerance will influence the degree to which an individual tends to swear. Their behaviour, however, will also be constrained by the situation such that they will be more likely to swear when casually hanging around with friends and less likely to Be in a classroom or meeting with their boss. Situation Strength • Some researchers have speculated that organizations are, definition, strong situations because they impose rules, norms, and standards that govern behaviour. • But that does not mean it is always desirable for organizations to create strong situations for their employees due to the following reasons. Situation Strength 1. Jobs with numerous rules and tightly controlled processes can be dull or demotivating. 2. People do differ, so what works well for one person might work poorly for another. 3. Strong situations might suppress the creativity, initiative, and discretion prized by some cultures. One recent study, for example, found that in weak organizational situations, employees were more likely to behave proactively according to their values. 4. Work is increasingly complex and interrelated globally. Trait Activation Theory (tat) • tat. predicts that some situations, events, or interventions “activate” a trait more than others. E.g.: A commission-based compensation plan would likely activate individual differences in extraversion because extraversion more reward-sensitive, than, say, openness to new experiences. Trait Activation Theory (TAT) • A recent study applying TAT found that individual differences in the tendency to behave prosocially mattered more when coworkers were not supportive. supportive environment, everyone behaves prosocially, but in an environment that is not so nice, whether an individual has the personality to behave prosocially makes a major difference. Values • Values represent basic belief that a specific mode of conduct or end-state of existence personally socially preferable to an opposite or converse mode conduct end-state existence. Values • We enter an organization with preconceived notions of what “ought” and “ought not” to • These notions are not value-free; on the contrary, they contain our interpretations of right and wrong and our preference for certain behaviours or outcomes over others. Values • While values can sometimes enhance decision-making, at times they can also cloud objectivity and rationality. Regardless of whether they clarify or bias our judgment, our values do influence our attitudes and behaviours at work. Values • Dr Milton Rokeach, a Researcher -argued that we can separate values into two categories. 1. Terminal values Refer to desirable end states. These are the goals a person would like to achieve during his/her lifetime. E.g.: Economic success and prosperity Values 2. Instrumental values Refers to preferable modes of behaviour, or means of achieving the terminal values. E.g.: Personal discipline, Goal oriented • Each of us places value on both the ends (terminal values) and the means (instrumental values). • A balance between the two is important, as well as an understanding of how to strike this balance. Linking Values to Individual Personality at the Workplace • Today's organizations are very interested in knowing how well the individual's personality and values match the organization. • In other words, managers today are less interested in an applicant's ability to perform a specific job than in the applicant's flexibility to meet changing situations and commitment to the organization. Person-Job Fit • The effort to match job requirements with personality characteristics is best articulated in John Holland's personality-job fit theory. • Holland presents six personality types and proposes that satisfaction and the propensity to leave a position depend on how well individuals match their personalities to a job. Person-Job Fit • The closer two fields or orientations are the hexagon, the more compatible they are. • Adjacent categories are quite similar, whereas diagonally opposite ones are highly dissimilar. Person-Job Fit • Personality-job fit theory argues that satisfaction is highest and turnover lowest when personality and occupation are agreement. E.g.: A realistic person in a realistic job is in a more congruent situation than a realistic person in an investigative job. A realistic person in a social job is in the most incongruent situation possible. Person-Job Fit Person-Organization Fit • The person-organization fit theory essentially argues that people are attracted to and selected by organizations that match their values, and they leave organizations that are not compatible with their personalities. At the time of hiring organizations should identify new employees who fit better with the organization's culture, which should, in turn, result higher employee satisfaction and reduced turnover. International Values • Unlike personality, which as we have seen is largely genetically determined, values are learned from our environments. • Values are also shared between people and passed down from one generation to the next. • For these reasons, different value systems have developed over time in each national culture. title: 4 Emotions and Moods
content: Understanding Yourself & Others: Emotions and Moods. MN 4063: Organizational Behaviour & Management Nadeesha Perera Management Division Faculty of Engineering University of Moratuwa contents. • Four words! • It is only a matter of time! • The basic moods: Positive and Negative affect • The function of emotions and moods • Emotional labour • Affective Events Theory (AET) • Emotional Intelligence (EI) Four Words! Emotion: From the biological point of view, emotions are chemicals released in response to our interpretation of a specific trigger. From the OB perspective, emotions are intense feelings directed at someone or something. It takes our brains about 1/4 second to identify the trigger, and about another 1/4 second to produce the chemicals. Four Words! Emotion chemicals are released throughout our bodies, not just in our brains, and they form a kind of feedback loop between our brains and bodies. They last for about six seconds! Four Words! 2. Feelings: “Feeling,” it's something we sense. • Feelings happen as we begin to integrate the emotion, to think about it, to “let it soak in.” In English, we use “feel” for both physical and emotional sensation - we can say we physically feel cold, but we can also emotionally feel cold. Four Words! • Feelings are more “cognitively saturated” as the emotion-chemicals are processed in our brains & bodies. • Feelings are often fueled by a mix of emotions and last for longer than emotions. Four Words! 3. Mood A mood is a state of mind that tends to be less intense than an emotion and does not necessarily need a contextual stimulus. Mood is heavily influenced by several factors: the environment (weather, lighting, people around us), physiology (what we've been eating, how we've been exercising, how healthy we are), and finally our mental state (where we're focusing attention and our current emotions). Moods last longer than emotions, from hours to days. Four Words! 4. Affect This is a generic term covering broad range feelings people experience, including emotions and moods. It's Only a Matter of Time ! The short answer is: Time! Emotions come first, then feelings come after as the emotion chemicals go to work in our bodies. Then moods develop from a combination of feelings. The Basic Moods: Positive and Negative Affect There are 2 categories of emotions, 1. Positive emotions: Such as joy and gratitude, which express a favourable evaluation or feeling. 2. Negative emotions: Such as anger or guilt, which express an unfavourable evaluation or feeling. The two categories of emotions now represent overall mood states, known as positive and negative affect. The Basic Moods: Positive and Negative Affect • Positive affect as a mood dimension consisting of positive emotions such as excitement, enthusiasm, and elation at the high end (high positive affect), and boredom, depression, and fatigue at the low end (low positive affect, or lack of positive affect). • Negative affect is a mood dimension consisting of nervousness, stress, and anxiety at the high end (high negative affect), and contentedness, calmness, and serenity at the low end (low negative affect, or lack of negative affect). Experiencing Moods and Emotions Does the degree to which people experience positive and negative emotions vary across cultures? Your brain is wired for negative thoughts: Here's how to change it How to Deal with Negative Emotions: Daily Proven Techniques? The Function of Emotions and Moods • Organizational behaviourists have been finding that emotions can be critical to an effectively functioning workplace. • There are 2 critical areas where emotions can enhance performance. i.e. 1. Rationality and emotions 2. Ethicality and emotions Rationality and Emotions • As per the common belief, rationality and emotion are in conflict and that if you exhibit emotion, you are likely to act irrationally. • However, the research is increasingly indicating that emotions are critical to rational thinking. Rationality and Emotions • Brain injury studies in particular suggest we must have the ability to experience emotions to be rational. • Why? Because our emotions provide a context for how we understand the world around us. • A recent study indicated that individuals in a negative mood are better able to recognize truthful information than people in a happy mood. Rationality and Emotions • The keys are to acknowledge the effect that emotions and moods are having on us, and to not automatically discount our emotional responses as irrational or invalid. rational vs emotional behavior. by Rich Life Ethics (Moral attitudes) and Emotions Examples of moral emotions include sympathy for the suffering of others, guilt about our own immoral behaviour, anger about the injustice done to others, contempt for those who behave unethically, and disgust at violations of moral norms. Numerous studies suggest that moral judgments are largely based on feelings rather than on cognition, although assessments of fairness (which frequently influence moral judgments), do have a cognitive component. We tend to see our moral boundaries as logical and reasonable, not as emotional. Are Humans Emotional Creatures or Are We Rational? | Yale Psychologist Paul Bloom | Big Think Sources of Emotions and Moods • The primary influences can be grouped into two main types: 1. Influences based on who you are (such as age and personality) 2. Influences based on your circumstances at the time (such as time of day, your blood sugar level, etc.) 1. Influences Based on Who You Are 1. Personality: • Moods and emotions have a personality trait component: Most people have built-in tendencies to experience certain moods and emotions more frequently than others do. People also experience the same emotions with different intensities, which is called affect intensity. For e.g.: affectively intense people experience both positive and negative emotions more deeply: when they're sad, they're really sad, and when they're happy, they're really happy. 1. Influences Based on Who You Are 2. Age • One study of people ages 18 to 94 revealed that negative emotions appear less as people get older. • Periods of highly positive moods lasted longer for older individuals and bad moods faded more quickly. 1. Influences Based on Who You Are 3. Gender • Evidence does confirm women are more emotionally expressive than men, experience emotions more intensely, tend to “hold onto” emotions longer, and display more frequent expressions of both positive and negative emotions, except anger. 2. Influences Based on Your Circumstances at the Time 1. Time of the day Levels of positive affect are greatest in the evening, and lowest in the early morning, on most days of the week. • Levels of negative affect are also highest in the overnight hours, but the lowest point is later in the morning than for positive affect. 2. Influences Based on Your Circumstances at the Time 2. Day of the week • U.S. adults tend to experience their highest positive affect on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, and their lowest on Monday. This trend tends to be true in several other cultures as well. 2. Influences Based on Your Circumstances at the Time 3. Weather fairly large and detailed body evidence conducted by multiple researchers suggests that the weather has little effect, at least for most people. 2. Influences Based on Your Circumstances at the Time 4. Stress • Stressful events at work (a nasty e-mail, an impending deadline, loss of a big sale, a reprimand from the boss) negatively affect moods. • The effects of stress also build over time. • Mounting stress can worsen our moods such that we experience more negative emotions. 2. Influences Based on Your Circumstances at the Time 5. Social Activities • Research suggests physical activities (skiing or hiking with friends), informal (going to a party), or epicurean (eating with others) are more strongly associated with increases in positive mood than formal events (attending a meeting) or sedentary (watching TV with friends). 6. Sleep • Sleep quality affects mood, and increased fatigue puts workers at health risk of disease, injury, and depression. According to one study, poor sleep impairs job satisfaction because people feel fatigued, irritable, and less alert. 2. Influences Based on Your Circumstances at the Time 7. Exercise • Research consistently shows exercise enhances people's positive mood. • While not strong overall, the effects are strongest for those who are depressed. 2. Influences Based on Your Circumstances at the Time 8. Blood sugar levels • Low blood sugar occurs when someone has not eaten for too long. has been strongly associated with irritability, disagreeableness, and even combative behaviours. Excessively high blood sugar, too, most common among untreated diabetics, has been linked to depression. Emotional Labour • An employee's expression of organizationally desired emotions during interpersonal transactions at work. Emotional labour is a key component of effective job performance. • To analyze emotional labour, emotions are divided into felt or displayed emotions. Emotional Labour • Felt emotions are our actual emotions. • Displayed emotions are those that the organization requires workers to show and considers appropriate in a given job. • They're not innate; they're learned, and they may or may not coincide with felt emotions. Emotional Labour Displaying fake emotions requires us to suppress real ones. Surface acting is hiding inner feelings and emotional expressions in response to display rules. E.g.: A worker who smiles at a customer even when he doesn't feel like it is surface acting. Deep acting is trying to modify our true inner feelings based on display rules. Surface acting deals with displayed emotions, and deep acting deals with felt emotions. Emotional Labour • When employees have to project one emotion while feeling another, this disparity is called emotional dissonance. Emotional Labour Affective Events Theory • Affective Events Theory (AET) demonstrates that employees react emotionally things that happen to them at work, and this reaction influences their job performance and satisfaction. Affective Events Theory • People who score low on emotional stability are more likely to react strongly to negative events, and our emotional response given event can change depending on mood. • Emotions influence several performance and satisfaction variables, such as organizational citizenship behaviour, organizational commitment, level of effort, intention to quit, and workplace deviance. Affective Events Theory Emotional Intelligence (EQ) In 1983, Harvard Psychologist, Howard Gardner, put forward the theory of Multiple Intelligence, in which he argued that no single individual can be considered as an intellect or non-intellect based on a single test [Such as Intelligence Quotient (IQ)] when he/she is naturally born with multiple dormant abilities i.e. Linguistic intelligence Logical-Mathematical intelligence Musical intelligence Spatial intelligence Body-kinesthetic intelligence Intrapersonal intelligence Interpersonal intelligence Naturalist intelligence Howard Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligences Emotional Intelligence (EQ) In 1990 Peter Salovey and John Mayer, both eminent Professors of Psychology from the University of Yale and the University of Hampshire respectively gained a scientific interest in the concept by coining the term “Emotional Intelligence” for the first time by publishing a seminal article in the Journal- 'Imagination, Cognition and Personality' under the theme 'Emotional Intelligence'. Emotional Intelligence (EQ) • Mayer and Salovey viewed EI as an ability, skill or competency rather than a personality trait. Emotional intelligence (EQ) from an organizational behaviour perspective refers the ability individuals within workplace recognize, understand, and manage their own emotions and the emotions of others. Emotional Intelligence (EQ) • This skill plays a crucial role in enhancing teamwork, communication, and leadership effectiveness, ultimately contributing to a positive organizational culture and improved performance. • High emotional intelligence can lead to better conflict resolution, employee satisfaction, and overall productivity. Emotional Intelligence (EQ) Emotional Intelligence (EQ) Emotional intelligence (EI) is a person's ability to (1) perceive emotions in the self and others, (2) understand the meaning of these emotions, and (3) regulate his or her emotions Emotional Intelligence (EQ) • The Cascading Model of Emotional Intelligence is a framework that illustrates how various emotional intelligence skills develop and interact over time. Personal Emotion Regulation Strategies • Mindfulness Meditation: Practicing mindfulness helps increase awareness of your emotions and thoughts without judgment. This can lead to better emotional responses. • Cognitive Reappraisal: Change the way you think about a situation. Instead of viewing it negatively, try to find a positive angle or a lesson learned. Personal Emotion Regulation Strategies • Journaling: Writing about your feelings can help you process emotions and gain insights into your emotional triggers. • Breathing Techniques: Deep breathing exercises can help calm your mind and body, making it easier to manage intense emotions. • Physical Activity: Regular exercise can improve mood and reduce stress, making it easier to regulate emotions. Personal Emotion Regulation Strategies • Social Support: Talking to friends or family about your feelings can provide perspective and emotional relief. • Setting Boundaries: Learn to say no and set limits to protect your emotional well-being. • Practice Self-Compassion: Treat yourself with kindness and understanding, especially during difficult times. Personal Emotion Regulation Strategies • Develop Problem-Solving Skills: Addressing the root causes of your emotions can help reduce their intensity. • Seek Professional Help: If you find it challenging to manage your emotions, consider talking to a therapist or counsellor. Strategies Improve Emotional Intelligence in Organizations • Training Programs: Implement workshops and training sessions focused on emotional intelligence skills, such as self-awareness, empathy, and emotional regulation. • Coaching and Mentoring: Pair employees with mentors or coaches who can guide the development of EI skills through personalized feedback and support. Strategies Improve Emotional Intelligence in Organizations • Feedback Mechanisms: Establish regular feedback loops where employees can receive constructive feedback on their emotional interactions and behaviours. • Promote Open Communication: Encourage a culture of open dialogue where employees feel safe to express their emotions and thoughts without fear of judgment. Strategies Improve Emotional Intelligence in Organizations • Mindfulness Practices: Introduce mindfulness and stress management techniques to help employees become more aware of their emotions and reactions. • Team-Building Activities: Organize activities that foster collaboration and understanding among team members, enhancing their ability to empathize with one another. • Leadership Development: Train leaders to model emotional intelligence behaviours, as their actions set the tone for the rest of the organization. Strategies Improve Emotional Intelligence in Organizations • Diversity and Inclusion Initiatives: Promote a diverse workplace where different perspectives are valued, helping employees develop empathy and understanding. • Conflict Resolution Training: Equip employees with skills to manage and resolve conflicts constructively, focusing emotional awareness and communication. • Regular Assessments: Use tools and assessments to measure emotional intelligence levels within the organization and track improvements over time. Emotional Intelligence (EQ) People who are emotionally and socially intelligent can understand and express themselves, understand and relate well to others, and to successfully cope with the demands of daily life to do this effectively, they need to manage emotions and be sufficiently optimistic, positive, and self-motivated.

title: 5 Perception and Individual Decision Making
content: Perception and Individual Decision Making. MN 4063: Organizational Behaviour & Management Nadeesha Perera Management Division Faculty of Engineering University of Moratuwa contents. What is perception? Why 'Perception' is important in OB? Factors that influence perception The perception process Social perception: Judging others Individual decision-making Link between individual decision-making and perception Generally accepted constructs of decision-making in organizations Common biases and errors in decision-making Overcoming cognitive biases in business What is Perception? • Perception is a process by which individuals organize and interpret sensory impressions give meaning to their environment. • However, what we perceive can be substantially different from objective reality. What is Perception? • More commonly, people have very different impressions of their workplace even when their job tasks and working conditions are similar. Why 'Perception' is Important in OB? The world as it is perceived is the world that is behaviourally important. In general, people's behaviour is based on their perception of what reality is, not on reality itself. Factors that Influence Perception Factors that Influence Perception • Context / the situation matters: The time at which we see an object or event can influence our attention, as can location, light, heat, or situational factors. Factors that Influence Perception • The characteristics of the target. - Loud people are more likely to be noticed than quiet ones. - We also have a broad tendency to perceive people who we think are similar to us in positive ways and people who we think are different from us in negative ways. Factors that Influence Perception • Personal characteristics of the Perceiver- attitudes, personality, motives, interests, past experiences, and expectations. If you expect police officers to be authoritative, you may perceive them as such, regardless of their actual traits. Factors that Influence Perception People have inherent biases in how they see others (perception) and in how they make decisions (decision-making). We can better understand people by understanding these biases. The Perception Process The Perception Process 1. Receiving Stimuli : The stimuli are received from various sources, through the five organs. It is a physiological aspect of the perception process. Stimuli may be external to us (such as sound waves) and inside us (such as energy generation by muscles). The Perception Process 2. Selection of Stimuli : After receiving the stimuli or data, some are selected. Others are screened out. Two types of factors affect the selection of stimuli for processing: external and internal factors. External factors relate to stimuli such as intensity of stimuli, size, movement, repetition, etc. Internal factors relate to the perceiver such as his/her age, learning, interest, etc. Normally, he will select the objects that interest him and avoid those to which he is indifferent. This is also called 'selective perception'. The Perception Process 3. Organization of Stimuli : Organising the bits information into meaningful whole is called "organization". There are three ways by which the selected data (inputs) are organised. These are : Grouping Closure (iii) Simplification The Perception Process Grouping: In grouping, the perceiver groups the various stimuli based their similarity proximity. For example, all the workers coming from the same place may be perceived as similar based on proximity. Closure: When faced with incomplete information, people fill up the gaps themselves to make the information meaningful. This may be done based on past experience, past data, or hunches. The Perception Process (iii) Simplification: People identify the main stimulus features and assess how they are organized. He interprets a stimulus situation, the perceiver simplifies the information. Social Perception: Judging Others • Social perception is the process by which individuals gather and interpret information about other people through cues such as physical appearance, verbal communication, and nonverbal signals. This enables individuals to make judgments about social roles, relationships, and characteristics. Attribution Theory • Attribution theory explains the ways we judge people differently, depending on the meaning we attribute behaviour. Attribution Theory suggests that when observe individual's behaviour, attempt determine whether was internally externally caused. • That determination depends largely on three factors: (1) distinctiveness, (2) consensus, (3) consistency. Attribution Theory Internally caused behaviours are those an observer believes to be under the personal control of another individual. Externally caused behaviour is what we imagine the situation forced the individual to do. If one of your employees is late for work, you might attribute that to his overnight partying and subsequent oversleeping. This is an internal attribution. But if you attribute his tardiness to an automobile accident that tied up traffic, you are making an external attribution. Attribution Theory • Distinctiveness refers to whether an individual displays different behaviours in different situations. Is the employee who arrives late today also one who regularly blows off other kinds of commitments? What we want to know is whether this behaviour is unusual. If it is, we are likely to give it an external attribution. If it's not, we will probably judge the behaviour to be internal. Attribution Theory • If everyone who faces a similar situation responds in the same way, the behaviour shows consensus. • From an attribution perspective, if consensus is high, you would probably give an external attribution the employee's tardiness, whereas if other employees who took the same route made it to work on time, you would attribute his lateness to an internal cause. Attribution Theory • Consistency in a person's actions refers to 'Does the person respond the same way over time?' • The more consistent the behaviour, the more we are inclined to attribute it to internal causes. Coming in 10 minutes late for work is not perceived in the same way for an employee who hasn't been late for several months as it is for an employee who is late three times a week. Common Shortcuts in Judging Others • Selective perception • Halo effect • Contrast effects • Social identity effects • Stereotyping The Process of Perceptual Selectivity Perceptual selectivity is a cognitive process where individuals selectively attend to specific stimuli based on their relevance, importance, and personal interests. The Process of Perceptual Selectivity 1. Size: Bigger size attracts the attention of the perceiver. 2. Intensity: A loud sound, strong odour or bright light is noticed more as compared to a soft sound, weak odour or dim light. 3. Repetition: A repeated external stimulus is more attention-getting than a single one. Advertisers use this principle. 4. Novelty and Familiarity: A novel or a familiar external situation can serve as an attention-getter. The Process of Perceptual Selectivity 5. Contrast: It is a kind of uniqueness which can be used for attention-getting. Letters of bold types, persons dressed differently than others, etc., get more attention. 6. Motion: A moving object draws more attention as compared to a stationary object. Advertisers use this principle. The Process of Perceptual Selectivity Self-concept: The way a person views the world depends a great deal on the concept or image he has about himself. The concept plays an internal role in perceptual selectivity. Beliefs: A person's beliefs have a profound influence on his perception. Thus, a fact is conceived not on what it is but what a person believes it to be. Expectations: These affect perceptions. A technical manager may expect ignorance about a product's technical features from non-technical people. The Process of Perceptual Selectivity • Inner Needs: The need is a feeling of tension or discomfort when one thinks he is missing something. People with different needs experience different stimuli. • Response Disposition: It refers to a person's tendency to perceive familiar stimuli rather than unfamiliar ones. The Process of Perceptual Selectivity • Response Salience: the set dispositions which are determined not by the familiarity of the stimulus situations, but the person's cognitive predispositions. Thus, a particular problem may be viewed as a marketing problem by marketing personnel, a control problem by accounting people and a human relations problem by personnel people. The Process of Perceptual Selectivity • Perceptual Defence: It refers to the screening of those elements which create conflict and threatening situations in people. Denying the existence importance conflicting information. - Distorting the new information to match the old one. - Acknowledging the new information but treating it as a non-representation exception. Halo Effect • The halo effect is a cognitive bias where our overall impression of a person, brand, or product influences our feelings and thoughts about their other attributes. If someone is perceived as attractive or likeable, we may also view their skills or characteristics more favourably, regardless their actual performance. Contrast Effect The contrast effect cognitive bias that influences how we perceive differences between objects experiences. It occurs when our judgments are affected by comparing something to a contrasting reference point, thereby enhancing the differences between them. Social Identity Effect • The social identity effect refers to how individuals define themselves about social groups and how this identification influences behaviour, thoughts, and emotions. • It can enhance feelings of belonging and self-esteem and can impact attitudes towards in-group and out-group members. Stereotyping • Stereotyping refers to the generalized beliefs expectations about particular category of people, where individuals ascribe collective characteristics associated with specific group to every member of that group, often overlooking individual differences. Individual Decision Making • Decision-making occurs as a reaction to a problem. • Problem- A discrepancy exists between the current state of affairs and some desired state, requiring us to consider alternative courses of action. Link Between Individual Decision- Making and Perception • One person's problem is another person's satisfactory state of affairs. One manager may view her division's 2% decline in quarterly sales as a serious problem requiring immediate action. Her counterpart in another division, who also had a 2% sales decrease, might consider that quite acceptable. Link Between Individual Decision- Making and Perception Awareness that a problem exists and that a decision might or might not be needed is a perceptual issue. Generally Accepted Constructs of Decision-Making in Organizations • The rational decision-making model • Bounded rationality • Intuition The Rational Decision-Making Model • The rational decision-making model assumes that the decision-maker has complete information, can identify all the relevant options unbiasedly and chooses the option with the highest utility. The Rational Decision-Making Model • In reality, though, most decisions don't follow the rational model; people are usually content to find an acceptable or reasonable solution to a problem rather than an optimal one. • Most significant decisions are made judgment, rather than defined prescriptive model. Bounded Rationality • Many problems don't have an optimal solution because they are too complicated to fit the rational decision-making model, so people satisfice-they seek “satisfactory and sufficient.” • We tend to reduce complex problems to a level we can readily understand. Bounded Rationality • Bounded rationality human decision-making process which attempt to satisfice, rather than optimize. • In other words, we seek a decision that will be good enough, rather than the best possible decision. Intuition Intuition • Perhaps the least rational way of making decisions is intuitive decision-making, a non- conscious process created from concentrated experience. Intuitive decision-making occurs outside conscious thought; relies holistic associations, links between disparate pieces information; fast; and affectively charged, meaning it engages the emotions. Intuition • While intuition isn't rational, it isn't necessarily wrong. Nor does it always contradict rational analysis; the two can complement each other. • Nor is intuition superstition, or the product of some magical or paranormal sixth sense. • Intuition is complex and based on years of experience and learning. Intuition “Intuition can be very useful as a way of setting up a hypothesis but is unacceptable as 'proof.' Use hunches derived from your experience to speculate, yes, but always make sure to test those hunches with objective data and rational, dispassionate analysis”. Common Biases and Errors in Decision- Making • Overconfidence bias • Anchoring bias • Confirmation bias • Availability bias • Escalation of commitment • Loss aversion • Hindsight bias Overconfidence Bias • Recent research continues to conclude that we tend to be overconfident about our abilities and about the abilities of others, and that we are usually not aware of this bias. • Individuals whose intellectual and interpersonal abilities are weakest are most likely to overestimate their performance and ability. Overconfidence Bias • There's also a negative relationship between entrepreneurs' optimism and the performance of their new ventures: the more optimistic, the less successful. • The tendency to be too confident about their ideas might keep some from planning how to avoid problems that arise. Anchoring Bias Anchoring bias is a tendency to fixate on initial information and fail adequately adjust for subsequent information. other words, our mind appears give disproportionate amount of emphasis to the first information it receives. Anchors are widely used by people in professions in which persuasion skills are important-advertising, management, politics, real estate, and law. Anytime a negotiation takes place, so does anchoring. Confirmation Bias • Confirmation bias represents a case of selective perception: seek out information that reaffirms our past choices, and we discount information that contradicts them. We also tend to accept at face value information that confirms our preconceived views, while we are skeptical of information that challenges them. • Therefore, the information we gather is typically biased toward supporting views we already hold. Confirmation Bias • We even tend to seek sources most likely to tell us what we want to hear, and we give too much weight supporting information and too little contradictory. • We are most prone to confirmation bias when we believe we have good information and strong opinions. • Fortunately, those who feel there is a need to be accurate in making a decision are less prone to confirmation bias. Availability Bias Availability bias is our tendency to base judgments on information readily available. Recent research indicates that a combination of readily available information and our previous direct experience with similar information is particularly impactful to our decision- making. Events that evoke emotions, that are particularly vivid, or that are more recent tend to be more available in our memory, leading us to overestimate the chances of unlikely events such as being in an aeroplane crash, suffering complications from medical treatment, or getting fired. Escalation of Commitment • Escalation of commitment refers to our staying with a decision even if there is clear evidence it's wrong. • When is escalation most likely to occur? Evidence indicates that it occurs when individuals view themselves as responsible for the outcome. • The fear of personal failure even biases the way we search for and evaluate information so that we choose only information that supports our dedication. Loss Aversion • Loss aversion is a cognitive bias that indicates individuals feel the pain losses more intensely than the pleasure of equivalent gains, typically experiencing losses as psychologically twice as powerful. This concept highlights how outcomes are perceived as gains and losses, with losses having a more significant emotional impact. Hindsight Bias • Hindsight bias is the tendency to believe falsely after the outcome is known, that we would have accurately predicted it. When we have feedback on the outcome, we seem good at concluding it was obvious.

title: 6 Fundamentals of Group Behaviour
content: Fundamentals of Group Behaviour. MN 4063: Organizational Behaviour & Management Nadeesha Perera Management Division Faculty of Engineering University of Moratuwa contents. What is a group? Group classification The five-stage model Punctuated-equilibrium Model Group Roles Group Norms How do norms influence behaviour? Deviant workplace behaviour Group status Group size Group cohesiveness Group diversity Group decision-making What is a Group? A group is two or more individuals, interacting and interdependent, who have come together to achieve particular objectives. Group classification • Groups can be either formal or informal; both types affect employee behaviour and performance. • Formal Groups: A formal group is defined by the organization's structure, with designated work assignments and established tasks. In formal groups, the behaviours group members should engage in are stipulated by and directed toward organizational goals. Group classification • Informal Groups: An informal group is neither formally structured nor organizationally determined. Informal groups in the work environment meet the need for social contact. Four employees from different departments who regularly have lunch together or who meet to play squash on weekends are an informal group. These types of interactions among individuals, though informal, deeply affect their behaviour and performance. The Five- Stage Model- Tuckman Model Stage 1: Forming • Group members are polite and reserved as they get to know each other. • They seek clarity on the group's purpose, goals, and tasks. • There may be a sense of excitement and anticipation about the upcoming collaboration. • Group members tend to rely on the authority of the leader for guidance and decision-making. Stage 2: Storming • Conflicts and disagreements arise different viewpoints and ideas are expressed. • Power struggles and competition for leadership roles may occur. • Group members may challenge the leader's decisions and question the group's direction. • Communication might be strained, and there could be emotional tension within the group. Stage 3: Norming • Conflicts start addressed and resolved constructively. • Group members find common ground and establish norms for better collaboration. • Trust and camaraderie develop among the members, leading to improved communication. • Roles and responsibilities become clearer, and the group starts to operate more cohesively. Stage 4: Performing • The group achieves a high level of productivity and efficiency. • They work together seamlessly and effectively to accomplish tasks and goals. • Members understand each other's strengths and weaknesses, leveraging them for optimal performance. • The group becomes more self-managing, and decision- making is shared among members. Stage 4: Adjourning • The group acknowledges and celebrates their accomplishments. • They express gratitude and recognition for each other's contributions. • Members may experience a mix of emotions, including pride, nostalgia, and sadness, they say their goodbyes. • Individuals prepare to move on to new projects or join different teams. The Five- Stage Model- Tuckman Model • Many interpreters of the five-stage model have assumed that a group becomes more and more effective as it progresses through the first four stages. • Although this may be generally true, what makes a group effective is more complex. The Five- Stage Model- Tuckman Model • First, groups proceed through the stages of group development at different rates. • Some may even get stuck in a particular stage, such as storming, for extended periods. • Groups with a strong sense of purpose and strategy tend to rapidly reach the performing stage and improve over time, whereas those with less sense of purpose see their performance worsen over time. The Five- Stage Model- Tuckman Model • Similarly, groups that begin with a positive social focus achieve the performing stage more rapidly. It's also true that groups do not always proceed clearly from one stage to the next. • Storming and performing can occur simultaneously, and groups can regress to previous stages. Punctuated-Equilibrium Model • An alternative model for temporary groups with deadlines. E.g.: Classmates preparing a presentation for a semester-long class. • Studies indicate they have their unique sequencing of actions (or inaction). Punctuated-Equilibrium Model 1. Their first meeting sets the group's direction. The first phase group activity one inertia/inactivity and thus slower progress. 3. A transition takes place exactly when the group has used up half its allotted time. 4. This transition initiates major changes. 5. A second phase of inertia follows the transition. 6. The group's last meeting is characterized by markedly accelerated activity. Punctuated-Equilibrium Model • The punctuated-equilibrium model characterizes groups as exhibiting long periods of inertia scattered with brief revolutionary changes triggered primarily by members' awareness of time and deadlines. Group Roles • Work groups shape members' behaviour and help explain individual behaviour and the group's performance. • Some defining group properties are roles, norms, status, size, cohesiveness, and diversity. • A role is a set of expected behaviour patterns attributed to someone occupying a given position in a social unit. • We are required to play many diverse roles, both on and off our jobs. Role Perception • Role perception refers to how individuals define and understand their work roles, including the tasks, goals, and problems associated with those roles. • This perception significantly influences their behaviour and performance in the workplace, as it shapes how employees approach their responsibilities and interact with others. Role Expectations • Role expectations refer the behaviours and responsibilities that a group or society expects from an individual in a specific role. • These expectations define how the role should be performed and often include obligations associated with that role. • Clear role expectations help minimize confusion and set accountability for behaviours and performance. Role Conflicts • Role conflict occurs when workers are given different and incompatible roles simultaneously, or their role overlaps with another worker or work group. • The greater the role conflict, the higher the likelihood of a worker experiencing work-related stress. Group Norms • Group norms refer to the acceptable standards of behaviour shared by their members that express what they ought and ought not to do under certain circumstances (Social Rules). • Norms are distinct from rules, policies, and laws, which are formally enforced the legitimate hierarchy within an organization. • Norms, by contrast, emerge more naturally and influence behaviour with a minimum of external controls. Group Norms • Norms can cover any aspect of group behaviour. • Performance norms provide explicit cues about how hard members should work, how to do the job, what level of tardiness is appropriate, and the like. • Appearance norms - dress codes, unspoken rules about when to look busy etc. Group Norms • Social arrangement norms -with whom to eat lunch, whether to form friendships with coworkers off the job, whether to offer tobacco to a community elder before requesting their advice etc. • Resource allocation norms -assignment of difficult jobs, distribution resources like pay equipment. Group Norms Communication Norms: • Turn-Taking: Members may agree to speak one at a time during discussions. • Respectful Language: Using polite and respectful language expected foster positive environment. Group Norms Decision-Making Norms: • Consensus-Building: The group may strive for consensus before making decisions. • Respecting Majority Rule: Decisions may be made based on the majority opinion, with all members expected to abide by the outcome. How do Norms influence Behaviour? • Social sanctions in groups are mechanisms that enforce group norms and promote conformity among members. • They can be categorized into two main types: positive and negative sanctions. Positive Sanctions • These involve rewards or reinforcement for behaviours that align with group norms. Examples include: • Praise or Recognition: Members may receive compliments or public acknowledgment for adhering to group norms. • Increased Status: Individuals who consistently follow group norms may gain higher status or leadership roles. • Group Benefits: Participation in activities, resources, or support from other members as a reward for conforming behaviour. Negative Sanctions • These involve penalties or disapproval for behaviours that deviate from group norms. Examples include: • Social Ostracism: Exclusion from group activities or social interactions can occur for those who do not conform. • Criticism or Rebuke: Members may face direct criticism or negative remarks from others for violating norms. • Loss of Trust or Support: Deviating from group expectations can lead to a loss of trust, making it difficult for individuals to receive help or cooperation. Effects of Social Sanctions • Promote Conformity: They encourage individuals to align their behaviour with group norms to avoid negative consequences or gain positive rewards. • Reinforce Cohesiveness: Sanctions help maintain group identity and cohesiveness by ensuring that all members are aligned with shared values and standards. • Facilitate Control: They serve as a tool for group leaders or members to manage behaviours and maintain order within the group. Deviant Workplace Behaviour Deviant workplace behaviour (also called antisocial behaviour workplace incivility) voluntary behaviour that violates significant organizational norms and, in doing so, threatens the well-being of the organization or its members. Deviant Workplace Behaviour Causes of Workplace Deviance • Perceived Inequities: Feelings of unfair treatment regarding pay, promotion opportunities, workload can lead individuals to engage in deviant actions as a response. • Job Dissatisfaction: Employees who feel unfulfilled or unhappy with their roles may act out as a form of protest or rebellion.
