Causes of Workplace Deviance • Poor Organizational Culture: unhealthy workplace culture that lacks support, trust, or respect can normalize deviant behaviours. • Workplace Stress: High levels of stress or burnout may cause employees to behave in ways that are disruptive or harmful. Causes of Workplace Deviance • Leadership Quality: Ineffective or unsupportive management can contribute feelings disengagement, prompting deviant behaviour. • Social Norms and Peer Influence: If deviant behaviour is prevalent in a workgroup or tolerated by peers, individuals may feel socially pressured to conform. Causes of Workplace Deviance • Opportunity and Rationalization: Employees may act deviant if they believe they can do so without consequences and justify their actions acceptable. • Individual Differences: Personality traits like low conscientiousness, high impulsivity, or anti-social tendencies can predispose some employees to engage in workplace deviance. Consequences of Workplace Deviance Some research suggests a chain reaction occurs in groups with high levels of dysfunctional behaviour. The process begins with negative behaviours like shirking, undermining coworkers, or being generally uncooperative. As a result, the team collectively starts to experience negative moods. These negative moods result in poor coordination of effort and lower levels of group performance How can Workplace Deviance be Prevented? • Foster a Positive Culture: Encourage a respectful and inclusive workplace culture where employees feel valued and supported. Promote teamwork and collaboration. • Clear Policies and Expectations: Establish clear codes of conduct and policies regarding acceptable behaviour. Ensure employees are aware of the consequences of deviant behaviour. How can Workplace Deviance be Prevented? • Open Communication: Encourage open lines of communication where employees can express concerns without fear of retaliation. Regular feedback and dialogue can help address issues before they escalate. • Employee Engagement: Involve employees decision-making and initiatives, fostering a sense of ownership and pride their work. Engaged employees are less likely to deviate from workplace norms. How can Workplace Deviance be Prevented? • Conflict Resolution Mechanisms: Implement effective conflict resolution processes and provide training handling interpersonal issues constructively. • Support Systems: Offer resources such Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs), counselling services, and stress management training to support employee well-being. How can Workplace Deviance be Prevented? • Recognize and Reward Positive Behavior: Implement recognition programs reward employees for positive contributions and behaviour, reinforcing desired conduct. • Staff Training: Provide training on workplace ethics, communication skills, and teamwork to help employees understand the impact of their actions. How can Workplace Deviance be Prevented? • Monitor Work Environment: Regularly assess the workplace environment through surveys or focus groups to identify potential issues and areas for improvement. • Lead by Example: Management should model appropriate behaviour and demonstrate commitment maintaining positive work environment. Leadership plays a crucial role in setting the tone for workplace behaviour. Group Status • Status-a socially defined position or rank given to groups or group members by others- permeates every society. • Even the smallest group will show differences in member status over time. • Status is a significant motivator and has major behavioural consequences when individuals perceive a disparity between what they believe their status is and what others perceive it to be. What Determines the Status ? Status derives from one of three sources: The power a person wields over others: Because they likely control the group's resources, people who control the group outcomes tend to be perceived as high status. 2. A person's ability to contribute to group goals: People whose contributions are critical to the group's success tend to have high status. E.g.: Some thought NBA star Kobe Bryant had more say over player decisions than his coaches. What Determines the Status ? 3. An individual's personal characteristics: Someone whose personal characteristics are positively valued the group (good looks, intelligence, money, being an elder in Aboriginal communities, or simply having a friendly personality) typically has higher status than someone with fewer valued attributes. Status & Norms • Status refers to a person's accepted or official position within a social group, often indicating their rank or level of prestige compared to others. It encompasses both their social standing and the respect they command in various contexts. • Together, status and norms influence how individuals behave and interact in social groups, as norms provide guidelines for acceptable behaviour, and status can affect the power dynamics within a group. Status & Norms • High-status individuals are often given more freedom to deviate from norms than are other group members. • High-status people are also better able to resist conformity pressures than their lower-status peers. Research indicates an individual who is highly valued by a group but doesn't need or care about the group's social rewards is particularly able disregard conformity norms. Status & Norms general, bringing high-status members into group may improve performance, but only up to a point, perhaps because they may introduce counterproductive norms. Status & Group Interaction • High-status people tend to be more self-confident group members. They speak out more often, criticize more, state more commands, and interrupt others more often. • Lower-status members tend to participate less actively in group discussions. When they possess expertise and insights that could aid the group, failure to fully utilize these members reduces the group's overall creativity and performance. Group Size • Group size plays a crucial role in determining social dynamics, as the size affects the interactions and relationships between members. • Groups with a dozen or more members are good for gaining diverse input. • If the goal is fact-finding, larger groups should be more effective. • Smaller groups of about seven members are better at producing something concrete within deadlines. Social Loafing ( “Free Riding” ) • Social loafing is a phenomenon in social psychology where individuals tend to exert less effort when working in a group compared to when they are working alone. • This occurs because individuals may feel less accountable for the overall group's performance, leading to a decrease in individual effort. Causes of Social Loafing • Diffusion of Responsibility: In a group setting, individuals may feel that their personal contribution is less crucial, leading to a sense that others will pick up the slack. • Reduced Accountability: When working in a group, individuals may feel less personally accountable for the outcomes, as responsibility is shared among all members. Causes of Social Loafing • Lack of Identifiability: If individual contributions are not measured or recognized, individuals may be less motivated to put in effort. • Perceived Low Task Importance: If group members feel that the task is not significant or that their individual input won't make a difference, they may be less inclined to work hard. Causes of Social Loafing • Presence of Free Riders: Knowing that some group members may not contribute equally (free riders) can discourage others from fully engaging. • Group Size: Larger groups can increase social loafing, as individuals may feel less visible and less impacted by their personal lack of effort. Causes of Social Loafing • Group Culture: Negative group dynamics or a lack of cohesion can lead to decreased motivation and increased loafing. Social Loafing and International Cultures Social loafing appears to have a Western bias. It occurs more consistently within individualist cultures, such as the United States and Canada, which are dominated by self-interest. It does not occur consistently in collectivist societies, in which individuals are motivated by in-group goals. In studies comparing U.S. employees with employees from the People's Republic of China and Israel (both collectivist societies), the Chinese and Israelis showed no propensity to engage in social loafing and actually performed better in a group than alone. Steps in Minimizing Social Loafing (1) Set group goals, so the group has a common purpose to strive toward; (2) Increase intergroup competition, which focuses on the shared outcome; (3) Engage in peer evaluation, so each person evaluates the other person's contribution; (4) select members who have high motivation and prefer to work in groups; (5) if possible, base group rewards in part on each member's unique contributions. Group Cohesiveness • Group cohesion, also known as group cohesiveness or social cohesion, refers to the degree or strength of the bonds linking members of a social group. It is characterized by a sense of unity and connection among group members, enabling them to work together effectively toward common goals. Group Cohesiveness • Cohesiveness affects group productivity. • Studies consistently show that the relationship between cohesiveness and productivity depends on the group's performance-related norms. • If norms for quality, output, and cooperation with outsiders are high, for instance, a cohesive group will be more productive than a less cohesive group. Group Cohesiveness • If cohesiveness is high and performance norms are low, productivity will be low. • If cohesiveness is low and performance norms are high, productivity increases, but less than in the high cohesiveness/high-norms situation. • When cohesiveness and performance-related norms are both low, productivity tends to fall into the low-to-moderate range. Encouraging Group Cohesiveness (1) Make the group smaller. (2) Encourage agreement with group goals. (3) Increase the time members spend together. (4) Increase the group's status and the perceived difficulty of attaining membership. (5) Stimulate competition with other groups. (6) Give rewards to the group rather than to individual members. (7) Physically isolate the group. Group Diversity • Group diversity refers the inclusion individuals from various backgrounds, including but not limited to differences in age, gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and cultural perspectives within a team or organization. • This variety can enhance creativity, insight, and problem-solving but may also pose challenges in group dynamics. Group Diversity • Diversity appears to increase group conflict, especially in the early stages of a group's tenure, which often lowers group morale and raises dropout rates. • Culturally and demographically diverse groups may perform better over time-if they can get over their initial conflicts. Faultiness • Group faultiness refers to hypothetical dividing lines that may split a group into subgroups based on one or more attributes. An example of a strong faultline is a group of two young female Asians and two senior male Caucasians. Members' alignment of age, sex, and ethnicity facilitates the formation of two homogeneous subgroups. On the other hand, when a group consists of a young female Asian, a young male Caucasian, a senior female Caucasian, and a senior male Asian, the group faultline is considered weak because subgroups, regardless of how they are formed, are diverse. Faultiness Research on faultiness has shown that splits are generally detrimental to group functioning and performance. Subgroups may wind up competing with each other, which takes time away from core tasks and harms group performance. Groups that have subgroups learn more slowly, make more risky decisions, are less creative, and experience higher levels of conflict. Subgroups are less likely to trust each other. Finally, although the overall group's satisfaction is lower when faultiness is present, satisfaction with subgroups is generally high. Group Decision- Making Group decision-making is not always better than individual decision-making. Advantages of Group Decision-Making • Groups generate more complete information and knowledge. aggregating the resources several individuals, groups bring more input and heterogeneity into the decision process. • They offer increased diversity of views. This opens up the opportunity to consider more approaches and alternatives. Advantages of Group Decision-Making • Groups lead increased acceptance solution. Group members who participated in making a decision are more likely to support and encourage others to accept it enthusiastically. Disadvantages of Group Decision-Making • Group decisions are time-consuming because groups typically take more time to reach a solution. • There are conformity pressures. The desire by group members to be accepted and considered an asset to the group can squash any overt disagreement. • Group discussion can be dominated by one or a few members. they're low- and medium-ability members, the group's overall effectiveness will suffer. Disadvantages of Group Decision-Making • Group decisions suffer from ambiguous responsibility. In an individual decision, it's clear who is accountable for the final outcome. In a group decision, the responsibility of any single member is diluted. Groupthink & Groupshift Two by-products of group decision- making, groupthink and groupshift, can affect group's ability appraise alternatives objectively and achieve high-quality solutions. Groupthink • Groupthink relates norms and describes situations in which group pressures for conformity deter the group from critically appraising unusual, minority, or unpopular views. • Groupthink upsets many groups and can dramatically hinder their performance. Symptoms of Groupthink • Illusion invulnerability: Members feel overly optimistic and ignore potential risks. • Collective rationalization: Members dismiss warnings and negative feedback. • Belief in inherent group morality: Members believe their decisions are morally superior. • Stereotyping outsiders: Non-group members are viewed negatively. Symptoms of Groupthink • Pressure to conform: Members pressure dissenters to conform to the group's views. • Self-censorship: Individuals refrain from expressing their own doubts. • Illusion of unanimity: Silence is seen as consent. • Mind guards: Some members protect the group from dissenting information. Effects of Groupthink • Poor decision-making due to a lack of opposition and creativity. • Overconfidence among group members. • Groups may ignore critical information, which can exacerbate the risk of making unwise choices. • Groupthink can limit inclusion and the consideration of diverse perspectives, ultimately harming the overall effectiveness and profitability of group decisions. Does Groupthink Afflict All Groups? • Groups more focused on performance than learning are especially likely to fall victim to groupthink and suppress the opinions of those who disagree with the majority. • One study showed that those influenced by groupthink were more confident about their course of action early • Groups that believe too strongly in the correctness of their course of action are more likely to suppress disagreement and encourage conformity than are groups that are more skeptical about it. Preventing Groupthink • Encourage Open Dialogue: Create an environment where all members feel comfortable sharing their opinions and dissenting viewpoints. Emphasize that differing opinions are valuable. • Appoint a Devil's Advocate: Designate one or more group members to critically evaluate ideas and challenge assumptions, regardless of their personal views. Preventing Groupthink • Diverse Teams: Form teams with diverse backgrounds and perspectives to foster variations in thinking and minimize homogeneity. • Structured Decision-Making: Implement structured decision-making processes, such as brainstorming sessions nominal group techniques, to allow for the deliberate expression of ideas. Preventing Groupthink • Anonymous Feedback: Use anonymous surveys or suggestion boxes to allow members to express opinions without fear of judgment. • Encourage Independent Thinking: Foster organizational culture that values independent research and thinking before group discussions. Preventing Groupthink • Set Up Breakout Sessions: Divide the group into smaller subgroups discuss the issue independently before reconvening share findings. • Time for Reflection: Allow time for individuals to reflect on decisions and provide feedback after group discussions, ensuring that there is time to reconsider initial conclusions. Groupshift/ Group Polarization Groupshift/ Group Polarization • Group shift, also known as "groupshift," is a psychological phenomenon where the opinions and decisions of group members become more extreme than those they would make individually. This often occurs because group discussions can amplify individuals' pre-existing attitudes, leading riskier more cautious group decisions compared to solo decisions. Causes of Groupshift • Social Comparison: Individuals may adjust their opinions to align with what they perceive to be the dominant view within the group to fit in or gain approval. • Group Cohesiveness: High levels of cohesion can lead to a desire to maintain harmony, which may result in more extreme positions being adopted to strengthen group identity. Causes of Groupshift • Informational Influence: Exposure new arguments or persuasive rhetoric from group members can lead to a reevaluation of personal beliefs, pushing individuals towards more extreme views. • Desire for Distinction: Groups may adopt more radical positions to distinguish themselves from other groups, leading to shifts in attitudes and behaviours. Causes of Groupshift • Social Loafing: When individuals feel less accountable in a group setting, they may become bolder in their risk-taking behaviour, contributing to group polarization. • Lack of Accountability: Decision-making within a group can create a diffusion of responsibility, leading to more extreme positions. Group Decision-Making Techniques 1. Interacting groups 2. Brainstorming 3. Nominal group technique • Each of the group decision techniques has its own set of strengths and weaknesses. • The choice depends on what criteria you want to emphasize and the cost-benefit trade-off. 1. Interacting Groups • The most common form of group decision-making takes place in interacting groups. • Members meet face to face and rely on both verbal and nonverbal interaction to communicate. How a decision is ultimately taken within these groups can vary. • In Canada and other democratic countries, for instance, disagreements are often settled with a vote, with the majority getting their way. 2. Brainstorming • In a typical brainstorming session, a half-dozen to a dozen people sit around a table. • The group leader clearly states the problem so all participants understand. • Members then freewheel as many alternatives as they can in a given length of time. • To encourage members to “think the unusual,” no criticism is allowed, even of the most bizarre suggestions, and all ideas are recorded for later discussion and analysis. 2. Brainstorming • Brainstorming may indeed generate ideas-but not in a very efficient manner. • Research consistently shows individuals working alone generate more ideas than a group in a brainstorming session. • When people are generating ideas in a group, many are talking at once, which blocks the thought process and eventually impedes the sharing of ideas. 3. Nominal Group Technique • This technique restricts discussion interpersonal communication during the decision-making process, hence the term nominal. • Group members are all physically present, as in a traditional committee meeting, but they operate independently. 3. Nominal Group Technique Steps include, 1. Before any discussion takes place, each member independently writes down ideas on the problem. 2. After this silent period, each member presents one idea to the group. No discussion takes place until all ideas have been presented and recorded. 3. The group discusses the ideas for clarity and evaluates them. 4. Each group member silently and independently rank-orders the ideas. The idea with the highest aggregate ranking determines the final decision.

title: 7 Understanding work teams
content: Understanding Work Teams. MN 4063: Organizational Behaviour & Management Nadeesha Perera Management Division Faculty of Engineering University of Moratuwa contents. • What is a team? • Work groups vs. work teams • Types of teams • Multiteam systems • Creating Team Effectiveness • Turning Individuals into Team Players • Beware What is a Team? • A team is defined as a group of individuals who work together interdependently to achieve a common/shared goal or mission. • Unlike group, where members may coordinate their efforts without a shared aim, a team focuses on collaboration toward a specific objective. What is a Team? • A work team, generates positive synergy through coordinated effort. • The individual efforts result in a level of performance greater than the sum of those individual inputs. • A work team is a subset of a work group, the team constructed purposeful (symbiotic) in its member interaction. Work Groups Vs Work Teams • Both work groups and work teams may generate ideas, pool resources, coordinate logistics such work schedules. Types of Teams Problem-solving teams Self-managed work teams Cross-functional teams Virtual teams Problem-Solving Teams • Problem-solving teams are groups typically composed of 5-10 members from the same department who meet regularly to tackle specific business problems. • These teams often use a facilitator to guide discussions and generate a range of solutions, which can lead to more productive outcomes than what an individual might achieve alone. Self-Managed Work Teams • Self-managed work teams are groups of employees who organize and manage their own work without traditional hierarchical supervision. • These teams collaborate to plan, execute, and share responsibilities, operating in a self-directed manner achieve their objectives. Self-Managed Work Teams • Fully self-managed work teams even select their own members and evaluate each other's performance. • When self-managed work teams are established, former supervisory positions take on decreased importance and are sometimes eliminated. Cross-Functional Teams Cross-functional teams, made up of employees from about the same hierarchical level but different work areas who come together to accomplish a task. Cross-functional work teams are groups composed of individuals from various functional areas within an organization, such marketing, sales, product development, and customer service. Cross-functional teams are an effective means of allowing people from diverse areas to exchange information, develop new ideas, solve problems, and coordinate complex projects. Cross-Functional Teams • Due to the high need for coordination, cross- functional teams are not simple to manage. • Their early stages of development are often long, as members learn to work with the diversity and complexity. • The strength of traditional cross-functional teams is the face-to-face collaborative efforts of individuals with diverse skills from a variety of disciplines. Virtual Teams • A virtual team, also known as a remote or geographically dispersed team, is a group individuals who collaborate and communicate through electronic means rather than being physically present in the same location. • They utilize digital tools to work together effectively. Virtual Teams • For virtual teams effective, management should ensure that, Trust established among members (one inflammatory remark e-mail can severely undermine trust). 2. Team progress is monitored closely (so the team doesn't lose sight of its goals and no team member “disappears”), and 3. The efforts and products of the team are publicized throughout the organization (so the team does not become invisible). Virtual Teams Virtual teams face special challenges. They may suffer because there is less social rapport and direct interaction among members, leaving some members feeling isolated. The challenge of correctly dispersing information. Evidence from 94 studies involving more than 5,000 groups found that virtual teams are better at sharing unique information (information held by individual members, not the entire group), but they tend to share less information overall. Virtual Teams • The challenge of finding the best amount of communication. • Low levels of virtual communication in teams result in higher levels of information sharing, but high levels of virtual communication (meaning almost all communication is done online) hinder it. Multiteam Systems • Multiteam systems refer collections two more interdependent teams that together have a higher, shared goal. In other words, multiteam systems are a “team of teams”. • This lessens communication and coordination problems while still inviting participation from as many relevant parties as necessary. Multiteam Systems To picture a multiteam system, imagine the coordination of response needed after a major car accident. There is the emergency medical services team, which responds first and transports the injured to the hospital. An emergency room team then takes over, providing medical care, followed by a recovery team. Although the emergency services team, the emergency room team, and the recovery team are technically independent, their activities are interdependent, and the success of one depends on the success of the others. Why? Because they all share the higher goal of saving lives. Multiteam Systems • One study showed that multiteam systems performed better when they had “boundary spanners” whose job was to coordinate with members of the other subteams. • This reduced the need for some team member communication. • Restricting the lines communication was helpful because reduced coordination demands. Creating Team Effectiveness • Main assumptions of the 'Team Effectiveness Model' include, 1. Teams differ in form and structure. The model attempts to generalize across all varieties of teams but avoids rigidly applying its predictions to all teams. Use it as a guide. 2. Teamwork is preferable to individual work. Creating “effective” teams when individuals can do the job better is like perfectly solving the wrong problem. Creating Team Effectiveness 3. Team effectiveness includes objective measures the team's productivity, managers' ratings the team's performance, and aggregate measures of member satisfaction. The final outputs produced by the team must meet the standards set by key stakeholders, the internal social processes should enhance or maintain the group's ability to work together in the future, and the experience of working in a team environment should act to satisfy the personal needs of team members. Context • Adequate resources: Teams are part of a larger organization system; every work team relies on resources outside the group to sustain it. A scarcity of resources directly reduces the ability of a team to perform its job effectively and achieve its goals. This organizational support includes timely information, proper equipment, adequate staffing, encouragement, and administrative assistance. • Effective leadership and structure: Teams can't function if they can't agree on who is to do what and ensure all members share the workload. Agreeing on the specifics of work and how they fit together to integrate individual skills requires leadership and structure, either from management or from the team members themselves. Leadership is especially important in multiteam systems. Teams that establish shared leadership by effectively delegating it are more effective than teams with a traditional single-leader structure. Context • A climate of trust: Members of effective teams trust each other. They also exhibit trust in their leaders. Interpersonal trust among team members facilitates cooperation, reduces the need to monitor each other's behaviour, and bonds individuals by the belief that members won't take advantage of them. Members are more likely to take risks and expose vulnerabilities when they trust others on their team. Trust is the foundation of leadership; it allows a team to accept and commit to the leader's goals and decisions. • Performance evaluation and reward systems: Individual performance evaluations and incentives may interfere with the development of high-performance teams. So, in addition to evaluating and rewarding employees for their individual contributions, management should utilize hybrid performance systems that incorporate an individual member component and a group reward to recognize positive team outcomes. Team Composition • Abilities of members: Part of a team's performance depends on the knowledge, skills, and abilities of individual members. A team's performance is not merely the sum of its individual members' abilities. However, these abilities influence what members can do and how effectively they will perform on a team. High-ability teams are also more adaptable to changing situations; they can more effectively apply existing knowledge to new problems. • Personality of members: Some dimensions identified in the Big Five personality model are relevant to team effectiveness. Specifically, teams that rate higher mean levels conscientiousness and openness to experience tend to perform better, and the minimum level of team member agreeableness also matters: teams do worse when they include one or more highly disagreeable members. This relates to the concept of emotional contagion. Team Composition • Allocation of roles: Members should be selected to ensure all the various team roles are filled. Managers should assign the most able, experienced, and conscientious workers to the central roles in a team. • Diversity of members: People with diverse perspectives are likely to be more creative and innovative as a team because they will have a broader range of knowledge, information, and life experience to draw on when considering alternatives and proposing solutions. This positive influence is more likely to occur when the members respect each other's viewpoints and have strong communication skills. On the other hand, there is also a possibility that turnover will be greater among those with dissimilar backgrounds because communication is more difficult and conflict is more likely. Increased conflict makes membership less attractive, so employees are more likely to quit. Team Composition • Size of teams: Most experts agree that keeping teams small is key to improving group effectiveness. Generally speaking, the most effective teams have five to nine members. Experts suggest using the smallest number of people who can do the task. When teams have too many members, cohesiveness and mutual accountability decline, social loafing increases, and people communicate less. Large teams have trouble coordinating, especially under time pressure. • Member preferences: Not every employee is a team player. Given the option, many employees will select themselves out of team participation. When people who prefer to work alone are required to team up, there is a direct threat to the team's morale and individual member satisfaction. This suggests that, when selecting team members, managers should consider individual preferences along with abilities, personalities, and skills. High-performing teams are likely to be composed of people who prefer working as part of a group. Team Processes • Common plan and purpose: Effective teams begin by analyzing the team's mission, developing goals to achieve that mission, and creating strategies for achieving the goals. Teams that consistently perform better have established a clear sense of what needs to be done and how. Members of successful teams put a tremendous amount of time and effort into discussing, shaping, and agreeing on a purpose that belongs to them both collectively and individually. This common purpose, when accepted by the team, becomes what GPS is to a self-driving car: It provides direction and guidance under any conditions. Further, effective teams show reflexivity, meaning they reflect on and adjust their master plan when necessary. A team has to have a good plan, but it also has to be willing and able to adapt when conditions call for it. Team Processes • Specific Goals: Successful teams translate their common purpose into specific, measurable, and realistic performance goals. Specific goals facilitate clear communication. They help teams maintain their focus on getting results. • Team efficacy: Effective teams have confidence in themselves; they believe they can succeed. Successful teams raise their beliefs about future success, which, in turn, motivates them to work harder. In addition, teams that have a shared knowledge of individual capabilities can strengthen the link between team members' self-efficacy and their individual creativity because members can more effectively solicit opinions from their teammates. Management can facilitate improving team efficacy by providing training to improve members' technical and interpersonal skills. Team Processes • Mental models: Effective teams share accurate mental models-organized mental representations of the key elements within a team's environment that team members share. (If team mission and goals pertain to what a team needs to do to be effective, mental models pertain to how a team does its work.) If team members have the wrong mental models, which is particularly likely in teams under acute stress, their performance suffers. The similarity of team members' mental models matters, too. If team members have different ideas about how to do things, the team will fight over methods rather than focus on what needs to be done. Social loafing: Effective teams undermine this tendency by making members individually and jointly accountable for the team's purpose, goals, and approach. Team Processes • Conflict levels: Conflict on a team isn't necessarily bad. Conflict has a complex relationship with team performance. Relationship conflicts-those based interpersonal incompatibility, tension, and animosity toward others-are almost always dysfunctional. However, when teams are performing non-routine activities, disagreements about task content-called task conflicts-stimulate discussion, promote critical assessment of problems and options, and can lead to better team decisions. The timing of conflict matters, too. Moderate levels of task conflict during the initial phases of team performance were positively related to team creativity, but both very low and very high levels of task conflict were negatively related to team performance. Effective teams resolved conflicts by explicitly discussing the issues, whereas ineffective teams experienced conflicts focused more on personalities and the way things were said. Turning Individuals into Team Players • Many people are not inherently team players, and many organizations have historically nurtured individual accomplishments. • Teams fit well in countries that score high on collectivism. Selecting: Hiring team players • When hiring team members, sure candidates can fulfill their team roles as well as technical requirements. • People who are open to new experiences, comfortable with ambiguity, empathetic, socially oriented, and engage in high levels of self-monitoring tend to be more effective at cross-cultural communication. Training: Creating team players • Training specialists conduct exercises that allow employees experience the satisfaction teamwork can provide. Workshops help employees improve their problem-solving, communication, negotiation, conflict-management, and coaching skills. Rewarding: Providing incentives to be a good team player An organization's reward system must be reworked to encourage cooperative efforts rather than competitive ones. Teams that switch from a competitive to a cooperative system do not immediately share information, and they still tend to make rushed, poor-quality decisions. Apparently, the low trust typical of the competitive group will not be readily replaced by a high trust with a quick change in reward systems. Rewarding: Providing incentives to be a good team player • Promotions, pay raises, and other forms of recognition should be given to individuals who work effectively as team members by training new colleagues, sharing information, helping resolve team conflicts, and mastering needed skills. • This doesn't mean individual contributions should be ignored; rather, they should be balanced with the contributions to the team. Beware! How do you know whether the work of your group would be done better in teams? Follow these 3 tests Beware! 1. Can the work be done better by more than one person? A good indicator is the complexity of the work and the need for different perspectives. Simple tasks that don't require diverse input are probably better left to individuals. Beware! 2. Does the work create a common purpose or set of goals for the people in the group that more than the aggregate individual goals? Many service departments of new-vehicle dealers have introduced teams that link customer service people, mechanics, parts specialists, and sales representatives. Such teams can better manage collective responsibility for ensuring that customer needs are properly met Beware! Are the members the group interdependent? Using teams makes sense when tasks are interdependent-the success of the whole depends on the success of each one, and the success of each one depends on the success of the others.
